VIDEO.title: The Hardest Words of Jesus (That Churches Ignore)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: …if he listens to you, you have won your brother.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 18:15-35. If your brother sins, show him his fault privately; then with one or two more; then tell the church; and if he refuses even the church, let him be as the Gentile and tax collector. What you bind and loose on earth shall have been bound and loosed in heaven; where two or three gather in Jesus' name, He is there. Peter asks whether forgiving seven times is enough; Jesus answers with the parable of the slave forgiven an enormous debt who would not forgive a small one.

Binding and loosing is the language of halakha, the rabbis' work of applying God's commands to everyday life. In context, Jesus gives His community authority to deal with sin where Scripture gives no detailed instruction, and promises to agree with them.

The steps are not new: they echo Leviticus 19:17, just before 'love your neighbor as yourself,' and the two or three witnesses of Deuteronomy 19:15. Jesus was not introducing new concepts but correctly interpreting God's word.

Peter likely knew a rabbinic limit of three times and stretched to seven. Jesus answers with the number of Lamech's boast in Genesis 4:24: as revenge was a way of life for Lamech, radical forgiveness must be a way of life for the church. Peter heard discipline; Jesus meant reconciliation.

The lesson: the discipline that Jesus commands for His church must be saturated in radical forgiveness, because the goal of discipline is reconciliation. Excommunication must leave the door open; forgiveness keeps it open.
QUOTES: The discipline that Jesus commands for His church must be saturated in radical forgiveness.
Just as revenge was a way of life for Lamech, so must radical forgiveness be a way of life for all of you in the church.
Forgiveness leaves the door open to reconciliation.
Not publicly in order to shame us, but privately in order to restore us.

method.p: When Jesus answers 'seventy times seven,' the teacher asks: is there a seventy-seven in the Old Testament? There is, in Lamech's song of revenge. A number can be a remez, a hint that brings a whole story with it.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Now if your brother sins, go and show him his fault, between you and him alone; if he listens to you, you have won your brother.
For where two or three have gathered together in My name, I am there in their midst.
Jesus *said to him, “I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.

left.text: “Now if your brother sins, go and show him his fault, between you and him alone; if he listens to you, you have won your brother.

right.text: ‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you may surely reprove your neighbor, and so not bear sin because of him.

lines.text: When Jesus says this, the disciples are meant to think of Leviticus 19:17, which comes just before the second part of the greatest commandment, 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18).
Confronting a brother privately is loving him as we love ourselves. It is the way we would want to be approached: not publicly in order to shame us, but privately in order to restore us.

left.text: But if he does not listen to you, take one or two more with you, so that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every fact may be confirmed.

right.text: “A single witness shall not rise up against a man on account of any iniquity or any sin which he has committed; at the mouth of two or three witnesses a matter shall be established.

lines.text: The disciples should have remembered Deuteronomy 19:15. Jesus was not introducing new concepts for His people; He was correctly interpreting God's word.

This is partly why He said He came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill (Matthew 5:17). The video takes 'abolish' and 'fulfill' as idioms for misinterpreting and properly interpreting.

src.text: Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall have been bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall have been loosed in heaven.

lines.text: Rabbis were constantly asked to interpret commands. God says no work on the Sabbath, but does not define work, so leaders would bind (prohibit) some activities and loose (permit) others.

Here the context is dealing with sin in the kingdom community. God provides authoritative liberty to walk out His commands where His word gives no clear instruction, and 'where two or three have gathered together in My name' He agrees (Matthew 18:20).

RESTORE.title: As the Gentile and the tax collector

src.text: And if he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church; and if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as the Gentile and the tax collector.

lines.text: Jesus means: excommunicate the sinner who refuses to hear and obey the church's correction. Disciplining unrepentant sinners is a must; sin left unchecked will undo the community from the inside out.
But excommunication is meant as a deterrent, not the offender's last opportunity. The door must stay open for someone to return with a repentant heart.
Jesus Himself welcomed Gentiles and tax collectors; Matthew was one (9:9-10).

src.text: Then Peter came and said to Him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?”

lines.text: Peter is weighing excommunication against what Jesus said in Matthew 6:14-15: if you do not forgive, your Father will not forgive you. If the church can remove someone, when may an individual?
He likely knew the rabbinic expectation of forgiving three times, so he reaches further. But he is looking for a demarcation line.

src.text: And Lamech said to his wives, / “Adah and Zillah, / Hear my voice, / You wives of Lamech, / Give ear to my word, / For I have killed a man for striking me; / And a boy for wounding me; / If Cain is avenged sevenfold, / Then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

lines.text: Lamech, a descendant of Cain, lives his life marked by Cain's sin. His two-line poem, often called the Song of the Sword, is a boast: revenge is a way of life for him, next-level revenge.
If someone wounds him, he kills that man on the spot. This is horrific to brag about.

left.text: If Cain is avenged sevenfold, / Then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

right.text: Jesus *said to him, “I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.

lines.text: Jesus takes Lamech's number and fills it with new meaning: just as revenge was a way of life for Lamech, so must radical forgiveness be a way of life in the church.
The Greek can mean seventy-seven times or seventy times seven; the Greek Old Testament uses the same phrase in Genesis 4:24. Either way the point is no limit.

The disciples heard the teaching on reconciliation but latched on to the discipline part, as if it were for purging troublemakers. Jesus was thinking about reconciliation, so brothers and sisters stay aligned with God's word and mission.
There may be a hint of Lamech in Peter's attitude: if they go out the door, good riddance. That is not Jesus' heart.

src.text: When he had begun to settle them, one who owed him ten thousand talents was brought to him.

lines.text: A talent was a huge sum, roughly six thousand denarii, and ten thousand was the largest Greek number word. The debt is meant to be unpayable, yet 'feeling compassion' the lord forgave it all (18:27).

src.text: But that slave went out and found one of his fellow slaves who owed him one hundred denarii; and he seized him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Pay back what you owe.’

lines.text: A denarius was about a day's wage (20:2). The fellow slave uses the same plea, 'Have patience with me and I will repay you' (18:29), and is thrown into prison.

DEBT.title: Should you not also have had mercy?

left.text: Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow slave, in the same way that I had mercy on you?’

right.text: And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

lines.text: What God calls us to is radical forgiveness and radical mercy as a way of life. Go back and look at the Beatitudes and the Sermon on the Mount.
Jesus closes, 'if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts' (18:35).
The discipline Jesus commands must be saturated in radical forgiveness, because the goal of discipline is reconciliation, whether today, tomorrow or some point in the future.

Just because reconciliation is not possible with some folks in the moment, it does not mean forgiveness should not be extended. Forgiveness leaves the door open; there can be no expiration date on it.
If we are going to march forward together in unity (John 17), reconciliation must be one of the fundamental components of our community.

BACKGROUND.h: Binding and loosing in the rabbis
BACKGROUND.p: In rabbinic literature 'bind' and 'loose' are standard terms for forbidding and permitting. Jesus gave the same authority to Peter (16:19) and here to the community, in the setting of sin and discipline.

The closest written source is a saying in the Babylonian Talmud: 'When a person commits a transgression the first time, he is forgiven; a second time, he is forgiven; a third time, he is forgiven; but the fourth time, he is not forgiven' (Talmud Yoma 86b). It cites Amos 2:6 and speaks of God's forgiveness.

Selling a debtor with his family (18:25) reflects ancient practice, which the Torah limited for Israelites (Leviticus 25:39-43). A king's official owing ten thousand talents would be beyond any repayment.

WITNESSES.text: He did not say, You have a sufficient revenge, but, You have gained your brother, to show that there is a common loss from the enmity.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 60, on 18:15. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: not setting a number here, but what is infinite and perpetual and forever.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 61, on 18:22. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Two things therefore does He here require, both to condemn ourselves for our sins, and to forgive others
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 61, on 18:35. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: The Greek hebdomēkontakis hepta can mean 77 (as in the Greek of Genesis 4:24) or 490. The LSB has 'seventy times seven'; the video reads 77. Both point beyond counting.

The video takes 'abolish' and 'fulfill' (5:17) as rabbinic idioms for misinterpreting and correctly interpreting the Law. Some scholars hold this view; others read 'fulfill' as bringing the Law and Prophets to their goal in Jesus.
In 16:19 the words are spoken to Peter, in 18:18 to the disciples ('you' plural). Traditions differ on how the authority passes to church leaders or the whole congregation.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video reads 'seventy-seven times' in 18:22; the LSB has 'up to seventy times seven.' The Greek allows either.
The video's text of 18:15 says 'sins against you'; the LSB has 'if your brother sins,' because many early manuscripts lack 'against you.'
The rabbinic 'three times' limit is stated without a source. The closest text, Talmud Yoma 86b, is about God forgiving repeated transgression, not forgiving a brother.
Reading 'abolish' and 'fulfill' as Hebrew idioms for interpretation is one scholarly view, not a settled one.

The captions write 'hahikic,' 'hakic' and 'halaka' for halakha and halakhic, 'rebbitic' and 'rabbitic' for rabbinic, 'Kane' for Cain, 'Ada and Zilla' for Adah and Zillah, and 'biatitudes' for Beatitudes.

QUESTIONS: Why does Jesus start with a private conversation rather than a public one?
How does Leviticus 19:17-18 connect correcting someone with loving them?
What did Peter's question reveal about how he heard Jesus' teaching?
How does Lamech's song change the way you hear 'seventy times seven'?
Is there someone for whom you have put an expiration date on forgiveness?
How can a church practice discipline and still keep the door open?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: the discipline that Jesus commands for His church must be saturated in radical forgiveness, because the goal of discipline is reconciliation. Forgiveness and mercy are in short supply in many churches; hot takes, rage-baiting and cancelling people have crept in from the culture, and that can naturally follow from the spirit behind Peter's question. The teacher shares a pastoral story of a colleague who would not talk with hurting former members again, and warns that many Christians believe they are being righteous in their unwillingness to reconcile. Saturate your interactions with radical forgiveness and radical mercy, especially when dealing with someone else's sin.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): before you speak to anyone else about a hurt, ask whether you have gone to the person 'between you and him alone' (18:15). Pray Matthew 6:12 slowly, naming one person.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 18:15-35. If your brother sins, show him his fault privately; then with one or two more; then tell the church; and if he refuses even the church, let him be as the Gentile and tax collector. What you bind and loose on earth shall have been bound and loosed in heaven; where two or three gather in Jesus' name, He is there. Peter asks whether forgiving seven times is enough; Jesus answers with the parable of the slave forgiven an enormous debt who would not forgive a small one.
- Binding and loosing is the language of halakha, the rabbis' work of applying God's commands to everyday life. In context, Jesus gives His community authority to deal with sin where Scripture gives no detailed instruction, and promises to agree with them.
- The steps are not new: they echo Leviticus 19:17, just before 'love your neighbor as yourself,' and the two or three witnesses of Deuteronomy 19:15. Jesus was not introducing new concepts but correctly interpreting God's word.
- Peter likely knew a rabbinic limit of three times and stretched to seven. Jesus answers with the number of Lamech's boast in Genesis 4:24: as revenge was a way of life for Lamech, radical forgiveness must be a way of life for the church. Peter heard discipline; Jesus meant reconciliation.
- The lesson: the discipline that Jesus commands for His church must be saturated in radical forgiveness, because the goal of discipline is reconciliation. Excommunication must leave the door open; forgiveness keeps it open.

### Hear the number
When Jesus answers 'seventy times seven,' the teacher asks: is there a seventy-seven in the Old Testament? There is, in Lamech's song of revenge. A number can be a remez, a hint that brings a whole story with it.

   (video) What God calls us to is radical forgiveness and radical mercy as a way of life. Go back and look at the Beatitudes and the Sermon on the Mount.
   [Background] Jesus closes, 'if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts' (18:35). (Matthew 18:35)
4. The lesson: Saturated in radical forgiveness
   (video) The discipline Jesus commands must be saturated in radical forgiveness, because the goal of discipline is reconciliation, whether today, tomorrow or some point in the future.
   (video) Just because reconciliation is not possible with some folks in the moment, it does not mean forgiveness should not be extended. Forgiveness leaves the door open; there can be no expiration date on it.
   (video) If we are going to march forward together in unity (John 17), reconciliation must be one of the fundamental components of our community. (John 17:21)

## Key people
- Simon Peter: Asks whether seven times is enough; often the spokesman for the disciples. [Background] Later he writes, 'love covers a multitude of sins' (1 Peter 4:8).
- Lamech: Cain's descendant who boasts of seventy-sevenfold revenge. [Background] Fifth from Cain; the first man in Scripture with two wives (Genesis 4:19).
- Adah and Zillah: Lamech's wives, who hear his song. [Background] Mothers of Jabal, Jubal and Tubal-cain (Genesis 4:20-22).
- The forgiven slave: In Jesus' parable, forgiven a vast debt but unwilling to forgive a small one. [Background] His lord hands him over 'until he should repay all' (18:34).
- Cain: Lamech's ancestor, avenged sevenfold. [Background] God set a sign on him so no one would kill him (Genesis 4:15).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: The teaching continues in the house (Mark 9:33); Jesus leaves Galilee next (19:1).
- Bethsaida: Peter's hometown (John 1:44).
- Magdala: A fishing town on the west shore.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital on the lake.

## Key terms
- Halakha: Jewish legal interpretation: how to walk out God's commands in everyday life. The captions write 'halaka' and 'hahikic.'
- Binding and loosing: Prohibiting and permitting; here, the church's authority in dealing with sin.
- Excommunication: Removing an unrepentant member from the community, with the door left open to return.
- Song of the Sword: A common name for Lamech's boast in Genesis 4:23-24.
- Talent: A very large unit of money, about six thousand denarii. [Background]
- Denarius: A Roman silver coin, about a day's wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:2). [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Binding and loosing in the rabbis: In rabbinic literature 'bind' and 'loose' are standard terms for forbidding and permitting. Jesus gave the same authority to Peter (16:19) and here to the community, in the setting of sin and discipline.
- The 'three times' rule: The closest written source is a saying in the Babylonian Talmud: 'When a person commits a transgression the first time, he is forgiven; a second time, he is forgiven; a third time, he is forgiven; but the fourth time, he is not forgiven' (Talmud Yoma 86b). It cites Amos 2:6 and speaks of God's forgiveness.
- Debt and debt slavery: Selling a debtor with his family (18:25) reflects ancient practice, which the Torah limited for Israelites (Leviticus 25:39-43). A king's official owing ten thousand talents would be beyond any repayment.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "He did not say, You have a sufficient revenge, but, You have gained your brother, to show that there is a common loss from the enmity." Homilies on Matthew 60, on 18:15. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "not setting a number here, but what is infinite and perpetual and forever." Homilies on Matthew 61, on 18:22. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Two things therefore does He here require, both to condemn ourselves for our sins, and to forgive others" Homilies on Matthew 61, on 18:35. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Seventy-seven or seventy times seven? The Greek hebdomēkontakis hepta can mean 77 (as in the Greek of Genesis 4:24) or 490. The LSB has 'seventy times seven'; the video reads 77. Both point beyond counting.
- Abolish and fulfill as idioms The video takes 'abolish' and 'fulfill' (5:17) as rabbinic idioms for misinterpreting and correctly interpreting the Law. Some scholars hold this view; others read 'fulfill' as bringing the Law and Prophets to their goal in Jesus.
- Who binds and looses? In 16:19 the words are spoken to Peter, in 18:18 to the disciples ('you' plural). Traditions differ on how the authority passes to church leaders or the whole congregation.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video reads 'seventy-seven times' in 18:22; the LSB has 'up to seventy times seven.' The Greek allows either.
- The video's text of 18:15 says 'sins against you'; the LSB has 'if your brother sins,' because many early manuscripts lack 'against you.'
- The rabbinic 'three times' limit is stated without a source. The closest text, Talmud Yoma 86b, is about God forgiving repeated transgression, not forgiving a brother.
- Reading 'abolish' and 'fulfill' as Hebrew idioms for interpretation is one scholarly view, not a settled one.
- The captions write 'hahikic,' 'hakic' and 'halaka' for halakha and halakhic, 'rebbitic' and 'rabbitic' for rabbinic, 'Kane' for Cain, 'Ada and Zilla' for Adah and Zillah, and 'biatitudes' for Beatitudes.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why does Jesus start with a private conversation rather than a public one?
2. How does Leviticus 19:17-18 connect correcting someone with loving them?
3. What did Peter's question reveal about how he heard Jesus' teaching?
4. How does Lamech's song change the way you hear 'seventy times seven'?
5. Is there someone for whom you have put an expiration date on forgiveness?
6. How can a church practice discipline and still keep the door open?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: the discipline that Jesus commands for His church must be saturated in radical forgiveness, because the goal of discipline is reconciliation. Forgiveness and mercy are in short supply in many churches; hot takes, rage-baiting and cancelling people have crept in from the culture, and that can naturally follow from the spirit behind Peter's question. The teacher shares a pastoral story of a colleague who would not talk with hurting former members again, and warns that many Christians believe they are being righteous in their unwillingness to reconcile. Saturate your interactions with radical forgiveness and radical mercy, especially when dealing with someone else's sin.
- Study note (added): before you speak to anyone else about a hurt, ask whether you have gone to the person 'between you and him alone' (18:15). Pray Matthew 6:12 slowly, naming one person.
